162.title: The Masnavi begins
162.hook: his student Husam al-Din asks for a book, and Rumi dictates about 25,000 couplets in six books
162.howItsDone: The Masnavi is read aloud and taught in study circles in Iran, Afghanistan, Turkey and South Asia, often a few couplets at a time with a teacher's commentary, and the Mevlevi tradition gives it a central place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shams vanished, and Rumi signed thousands of poems with his friend's name. Your line was the grief sang.

Ever had a friend ask you for something that changed your life? Can you help me move. Will you coach the team. You should really write that down. Most of the time you say yes and forget. Sometimes the yes lasts years. Around 1258 in Konya, a devoted student of Rumi's named Husam al-Din came to him with a request. You've written thousands of short poems, he said. Your students love the long teaching poems of the older Sufi masters. Write us a book like that. Rumi said yes, and kept at it, on and off, for about fifteen years. Today's word is masnavi.
screen: `YOU SHOULD WRITE THAT DOWN.` → `HUSAM AL-DIN'S REQUEST.` → `MASNAVI.`

segments.voice: Masnavi is first the name of a form. In Persian poetry, a masnavi is a long poem in rhyming couplets: each pair of lines rhymes with itself, then the next pair takes a new rhyme, so a poem can run as long as a story needs. The word comes from an Arabic root meaning two, or in pairs. Poets before Rumi, like Sanai and Attar, had used the form for great teaching poems, and those were the books Husam had in mind. Rumi's became so famous that people often just call it the Masnavi, as if there were no other. A story people tell: when Husam asked, Rumi reached into his turban and pulled out a paper with the first eighteen lines already written. Charming, and probably legend. Better attested is how the rest was made. Rumi spoke it aloud, often at night, sometimes while walking or listening to music, and Husam wrote it down and read it back so Rumi could correct it. After the first book came a pause of about two years, when Husam's wife died. Then it went on. Six books. Around twenty-five thousand couplets. Stories of kings and grocers, lions and parrots, woven with verses of the Qur'an and teaching about the soul. The sixth book breaks off unfinished; Rumi died in 1273. This camp will read from it for months, story by story, so today is page one. The long book begins not with genius, but with a friend asking, and someone saying yes.

segments.voice: Think of something long that's been waiting for you: a big book, a language, a garden, a letter your kids will read when they're older. Don't plan the whole thing; just picture the first page, the first row, the first line, and decide what that first small step is, and when.

163.title: Keep him whole
163.hook: Rumi was a Muslim steeped in the Qur'an, and popular versions often strip that out; we won't
163.carry: a love he thought was wide
163.howItsDone: Sufi Muslims keep the daily prayers and the fast of Ramadan like other Muslims, and add practices of remembrance of God (dhikr), poetry and sometimes music, often in circles gathered around a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Masnavi began: a friend asked, and Rumi spoke six books aloud. Your line was begin the long book. Today closes the week.

In English, Rumi's lines turn up on wedding invitations, yoga studio walls and endless social posts. They're lovely. And some of them have had something quietly taken out. In some popular English versions, the mentions of God, of the Prophet, of the Qur'an, of the prayer he prayed five times a day, have been softened or dropped. What's left sounds like a poet from nowhere. But he was from somewhere. This week you've walked his road. Today's word is the name for the kind of Muslim he was: Sufi.
screen: `ON WEDDING INVITATIONS AND WALLS.` → `SOMETHING TAKEN OUT.` → `SUFI.`

segments.voice: A Sufi is someone on the inward, mystical path within Islam. The usual explanation is that the word comes from suf, Arabic for wool, for the rough wool robes some early ascetics wore. Others have proposed different roots, and nobody can settle it. Sufis aim to know God not only through law and learning, but through love, remembrance and the discipline of the heart. They pray the same prayers and keep the same fast as other Muslims; they add practices of remembrance, poetry and music, and they gather around teachers. Now put Rumi back together. The boy who walked west was the son of a Muslim preacher. The scholar of Konya taught Islamic law. The friend who arrived tested him with a question about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. And the Masnavi is so thick with verses of the Qur'an that tradition credits a later Persian poet, Jami, with calling it the Qur'an in the Persian tongue. When the reed flute you'll meet next week cries to go home, some readers hear a verse Muslims say at a loss. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." That's the ground his poems grow from. People from other paths, and none, love Rumi, and that's welcome here; he wrote about a love he thought was wide. But loving him well means meeting him whole. So in this camp, when he names God, the Prophet or a verse, i'll say so. Keep him whole.

segments.voice: The verse you just heard is what Muslims traditionally say when they hear of a death, or any loss: we belong to God, and to God we return. Hold that sentence for a minute without deciding what you think of it, just knowing that someone, somewhere, will say it today. Then look back over the week: the road west, the respectable one, someone arrives, the grief sang, the long book.

164.title: The emperor's notebook
164.hook: Marcus wrote in Greek, to himself, often on campaign, and the title "Meditations" came later
164.howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often keep it by the bed and read a single short section at a time, and many who follow modern Stoic practice keep their own journal of notes to themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the week closed with Rumi as he was: a Muslim, a scholar, a Sufi. Your line was a love he thought was wide.

Somebody opens your notes app. Not your posts, your notes. The reminders to yourself. Be patient with Dad. Stop checking your phone. You're not as tired as you think. A little embarrassing, and also a truer picture of you than any post. The emperor of Rome kept notes like that: reminders to himself, in Greek, some of them, it seems, written far from Rome on the Danube frontier, around the year 170. As far as anyone can tell, they were meant for no one else. Today, the emperor's notebook.
screen: `YOUR NOTES APP, NOT YOUR POSTS.` → `A TENT ON THE DANUBE, AROUND 170.` → `THE EMPEROR'S NOTEBOOK.`

segments.voice: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from 161 to 180. He spent much of his last decade at war along the Danube frontier, and it's likely that much of his notebook was written there, in camp. A few headings in the manuscripts seem to place him: one book ends with a note that it was written among the Quadi, a people on the far side of the river, and another reads: at Carnuntum, a Roman fort. Three things are worth knowing. First, he wrote in Greek, not Latin. Greek was the language of philosophy, and Marcus had studied the Stoics, among them the former slave Epictetus. Second, he wrote to himself. The notes scold, remind, encourage and repeat, the way you do when you haven't learned something yet. That's part of why they feel so alive: this isn't a man who has arrived; it's a man practicing. Third, the famous title isn't his. The old manuscripts carry a Greek heading usually translated to himself, and it may have been added by whoever copied the notes after his death. Meditations is what English readers later called the book. It survived by a thin thread of copies and was first printed in the 1550s. So beside Rumi this camp, remember the difference. Rumi spoke his book aloud to a friend who wrote it down. Marcus wrote his alone, for no one. Both, somehow, made it through the centuries.

segments.voice: Ask what you keep needing to remember and keep forgetting: be kinder to your sister, rest is not failure, finish before you start the next thing. Find one plain, honest sentence, the way you'd say it to a friend, and say it inside, slowly. If you can, write it down somewhere you'll see it again.

165.title: Book one: debts
165.hook: Marcus lists what he learned from each person, his grandfather's gentleness, his mother's simple living (Meditations 1.1–3)
165.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius, including people in modern Stoic practice, imitate book one by writing their own list of the people who formed them and the specific thing each one taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carnuntum: Greek notes by the Danube, written to himself. Your line was to himself.

The acknowledgments page usually sits at the back of a book. Thanks to my editor, my agent, my partner for putting up with me. It's easy to skip. Marcus Aurelius's notebook opens with its acknowledgments, and they fill a whole chapter. They aren't thanks for help with the book. They're thanks for help with becoming a person. Before a single piece of advice, he lists the people who shaped him, and exactly what each one gave. Today, book one: debts.
screen: `THE PAGE AT THE BACK.` → `A WHOLE CHAPTER OF THANKS.` → `BOOK ONE.`

segments.voice: Book one of the Meditations is seventeen short sections, and nearly every one starts the same way: from so-and-so, I learned this. It opens with his grandfather. In George Long's 1862 translation: "From my grandfather Verus I learned good morals and the government of my temper." Then his father, who died when Marcus was small, remembered for modesty and a manly character. Then his mother, and this one is lovely. From her he learned piety and generosity, to hold back not only from doing wrong but even from thinking it, and, in Long's words, "simplicity in my way of living, far removed from the habits of the rich." An emperor, thanking his mother for teaching him to live simply. The list keeps going. A tutor who taught him to put up with work and want little. A teacher named Rusticus who taught him to read carefully, not to settle for skimming, and who lent him the writings of Epictetus. Friends, philosophers, his adoptive father, the gods. Notice the order. Marcus doesn't start with who he is. He starts with who he owes. Every good habit traces back to a face: the opposite of the self-made man. And notice how specific he is. Not thanks, Mom. Thanks for this exact thing. Gratitude gets real when it gets specific. Your line is the question the whole book asks: from whom I learned.
screen: `FROM SO-AND-SO, I LEARNED THIS.` · `GRANDFATHER: GOVERNING HIS TEMPER.` · `MOTHER: SIMPLE LIVING.` · `NOT SELF-MADE: SPECIFIC DEBTS.` · then, large: `FROM WHOM I LEARNED.`

segments.voice: Let three people come, one at a time: a parent, a grandparent, a coach, a boss, a friend. For each, be as exact as Marcus, not they were great but what, exactly, they gave you, like a way of laughing at trouble, showing up early, how to make soup. Say each one inside: from them, I learned this.

166.title: The song of the reed
166.hook: the Masnavi opens with a reed flute crying for the reedbed it was cut from (Masnavi 1.1–18)
166.howItsDone: In the Mevlevi sema ceremony, the ney plays a central part, often opening with a solo improvisation, and the first eighteen couplets of the Masnavi, the song of the reed, are often recited and taught on their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, book one: Marcus listed his debts, one exact gift per person. Your line was from whom I learned.

There's a sound some people can't hear without their chest tightening. A cello. A train whistle at night. A certain voice on an old recording. It isn't even sad on purpose, and yet it opens something. In the Mevlevi ceremonies of Konya, the ones people call the whirling dervishes, the music often begins with one breathy, low, wavering flute, alone. It sounds like someone missing someone. Rumi's great book begins with that sound, and its verse opens with one word: listen. Today's word is the flute: ney.
screen: `A SOUND THAT OPENS SOMETHING.` → `ONE FLUTE, ALONE.` → `NEY.`

segments.voice: The ney is a simple thing: a hollow reed, cut from a reedbed, with holes burned into it. You blow across the top, and your breath becomes a voice. It's been played across the Persian, Arab and Turkish worlds for centuries. And in the opening lines of the Masnavi, it talks. In E. H. Whinfield's 1898 translation, the book begins: "Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains." Its complaint is separation. Ever since it was cut from the reedbed, the reed says, its crying has made men and women weep. It wants a heart torn by parting, someone who knows what being cut off means, so it can tell them the pain of longing. And its song, it says, is not wind. It's fire. One way readers hear it: the reed is the human soul, taken from where it began, near God, and set down in this world. The crying is the longing to go back. And the music, the thing that makes people weep, only happens because of the cutting. No reedbed, no flute. No separation, no song. Some read the reed as Rumi himself, the man who lost Shams and found his voice. Some hear the saint or teacher, emptied so that another's breath can play through. The poem lets all three stand. Rumi begins his life's great book not with an argument but with a sound: something cut from the reedbed, and singing because of it.
screen: `A HOLLOW REED, HOLES BURNED IN.` · `THE FIRST WORD: LISTEN.` · `IT CRIES FOR THE REEDBED.` · `NO SEPARATION, NO SONG.` · then, large: `CUT FROM THE REEDBED.`

segments.voice: Play one sad song you love, or, if you can find one, a recording of a ney, and do nothing else: don't sing along, don't scroll. Notice where it lands in your body and what it makes you miss. You don't have to name it; let the song say it for you, the way the reed does.

167.title: Whoever is far from home
167.hook: the reed says everyone parted from their source longs to go back (Masnavi 1.4)
167.howItsDone: The fourth couplet of the Masnavi is one of its most quoted lines in Persian, and Sufi teachers often explain it as the soul's longing to return to God, its source.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ney, the reed flute that opens the Masnavi crying for home. Your line was cut from the reedbed.

Homesickness is a strange feeling. You can be in a perfectly nice place, a good job, a new city, a dorm room with a fresh coat of paint, and some afternoon it hits: the smell of your grandmother's kitchen, the sound of a language you don't hear anymore. It aches. And it tells you something: which way home is. In the fourth couplet of the Masnavi, the reed stops describing its own pain and says something about everyone. Today, whoever is far from home.
screen: `HOMESICK IN A NICE PLACE.` → `THE ACHE POINTS SOMEWHERE.` → `WHOEVER IS FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the couplet, in plain words. Whoever is left far from their source longs to return to the time of being joined with it. Two lines, and they carry the whole book. The key word in Persian is asl: root, origin, source, the place something truly comes from. The reed's asl is the reedbed. Yesterday, one reading took the reed as the soul; today the reed names the place it misses. In the Sufi reading, that asl is God, and the longing people feel for something they can't name is a pull back toward it. Muslims hear a verse of the Qur'an under it: we belong to God, and to God we return. Here's the turn Rumi makes. Longing usually feels like a problem: something to get over, to fix, to scroll past. For Rumi it's the opposite. The ache is information, a compass needle. The reed wouldn't cry if it didn't remember the reedbed, and it wouldn't remember the reedbed if it weren't made from it. The longing is proof of the belonging. You don't have to share Rumi's faith to find this useful. When a longing comes that you can't place, you can ask not how do I make this stop, but which way is it pointing: toward a person, a place, a kind of work, a kind of quiet, God. Longing isn't only pain. Longing is a direction.

segments.voice: Let a longing come up, big or small: for a person, a place, a time, a feeling you once had. Don't push it away or feed it with a story; just sit next to it, the way you'd sit next to a friend who's sad. Then ask it gently, which way are you pointing, and whatever comes, or doesn't, is fine.

168.title: Near the lament
168.hook: the reed's secret is not far from its crying, but the ear and eye don't catch it (Masnavi 1.7)
168.howItsDone: Sufi teachers often read these opening couplets of the Masnavi as a lesson about hearing with the heart, and they are recited and explained couplet by couplet in study circles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asl: whoever is far from their source longs to return to it. Your line was longing is a direction.

You tell a friend something hard. Before you've finished, they're already answering. Have you tried therapy. My cousin had that. At least it's not worse. They mean well. But you walk away lonelier than before, because nobody actually heard the thing. And it's easy to be that friend too, the one waiting for a gap to talk. The reed in Rumi's poem knows this feeling. Everyone gathers around its music, and hardly anyone hears what it's saying. Today, near the lament.

A few couplets into the Masnavi, the reed says two things. First, in the sixth couplet: everyone became my friend from their own guess, and nobody looked for the secrets inside me. People liked the sad, beautiful sound and made it about themselves. Then the seventh: my secret is not far from my lament, but eye and ear do not have that light. The secret isn't hidden somewhere else. It's right there, in the crying. Anyone could hear it, but ordinary seeing and ordinary hearing miss it. The Persian word for the lament is nala: a moan, a cry, a sound of pain. Here's one way to hear it. The truth of a person, or of a soul, can sit right next to their sorrow. Not behind it. Not after it's fixed. In it. Sufi teachers read this about the soul's longing for God, which you can only understand from the inside, with a kind of inner light. But it works on a Tuesday too. What a friend most needs you to understand is often not far from what they're upset about. Rush to fix the crying, and you walk right past the secret. So how do you hear it? Slower. Fewer answers. More questions, like: what's that like? You keep your eyes and ears on the lament long enough for the light to come on.
screen: `FRIENDS FROM THEIR OWN GUESS.` · `THE SECRET IS NEAR THE LAMENT.` · `NALA: A MOAN, A CRY.` · `DON'T RUSH PAST THE CRYING.` · then, large: `LISTEN TO THE LAMENT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone carrying something right now, and picture them telling you about it.
